title: Cognitive Load, Three Ways
intro: “Reduce cognitive load” is too blunt. Sweller's theory splits it into three kinds, and each one calls for a different response.

learn.title: Three kinds of load
learn.text:
**Intrinsic** — the task's own complexity. Calculating returns is harder than reading a price. You can't remove it; you can chunk it.

**Extraneous** — effort caused by the design: clutter, poor layout, jargon. **Remove this.**

**Germane** — effort that builds a useful mental model. Support it with consistent patterns.

try.q: A tax form is hard because tax is hard. Which load is that?
try.explain: You can chunk it into steps, but you can't design it away.

left.label: Can't remove
items: Intrinsic: the task is genuinely hard
Chunk it across steps or screens

learn.title: The hospital example
learn.text:
On a hospital medication system, nurses faced medication lists, patient details and schedules crammed onto one screen.

Fieldwork showed the **intrinsic** load was unavoidable. The team **chunked** information across screens to cut the extraneous load, and simplified the language to support learning.

Errors dropped and efficiency rose. Nurses disliked the change at first; within a few months they were fully on board.

try.q: What does the hospital example suggest about user reaction to load reduction?
options: Initial dislike doesn't mean the change is wrong
Users always prefer fewer items per screen
Clinical users resist all interface change
try.explain: Errors dropped and efficiency rose; acceptance followed within months.

learn.title: Measuring it: NASA-TLX
learn.text:
When you need numbers, **NASA-TLX** measures perceived workload on six dimensions: mental demand, physical demand, temporal demand, performance, effort and frustration.

In practice: chunk complex tasks into steps, strip elements that don't serve the primary task, and use consistent patterns so effort goes into learning the domain rather than the UI.

options: The ratio of intrinsic to extraneous load
try.explain: It is a subjective workload instrument, not an objective timing method.

test.q: Where does cognitive load theory come from?
Which load should you remove outright?
options: All three, as far as possible
test.explain: It is effort the design added, serving nothing.

test.q: What do you do with intrinsic load?
options: Shift it to a help article
test.explain: The complexity belongs to the task; break it into steps.

options: Effort that builds a useful mental model
Load that varies by user expertise
The residual load after a redesign
test.explain: Support it with consistency so effort goes into the domain, not the UI.

test.q: Why is “reduce cognitive load” too blunt as advice?
options: Only one of the three kinds should be removed
Users differ too much for a general rule
test.explain: Cut the extraneous, respect the intrinsic, support the germane.
